synopsis: Published off-road acceptance targets remain sparse: ISO 16001:2017 is the only off-road standard found with hard detection and warning numbers, including 300 ms detection time; South Africa's braking regulation supplies no detection percentage, false-alarm limit or stopping test, while the MOSH surface specification requires at least 200 m detection range [f160, f165, f174, f2063, f2081]. No accepted off-road false-alarm rate was found, although ISO 21815-1:2022 requires physical performance tests with pass/fail criteria and a false-positive test; South African mine acceptance rests with the operator against the regulation, using industry guidelines as reference [f3605, f7726, f1367]. Automatic braking must be validated as a new safety-control function rather than against warning-system equivalence, with nuisance interventions weighted equally to missed interventions and stopping distance assessed against ISO 3450 or MOSH requirements [f10417, f10476, f5931, f5443]. Acceptance thresholds, statistical tests, confidence levels and stopping rules should be fixed before testing or hardware arrival, and the program should define criteria approved by technical authority [f644, f6956, f10600]. Test sufficiency should follow the claim and safety-relevant error bounds at declared operating boundaries—not fixed test or virtual-site counts—and public literature alone cannot establish whether the proposed architecture meets company release criteria [f5201, f6169, f4113, f4975]. Expert recommendations call for mature acceptance metrics and assessor agreement, plus a statistical acceptance plan and supporting validation infrastructure, by mid-2027; the manufacturer should retain ownership of acceptance criteria even when implementation is outsourced or hybrid [f7592, f5616, f8765, f8771, f8797].

relations.note: Both identify ISO 16001 as the sole off-road source of hard detection and warning numbers.
Both report absent numerical acceptance limits in South Africa's braking regulation.
Both report no accepted off-road false-alarm rate found.
Both identify the unresolved operator-acceptable off-road false-alarm rate.
Glossary entries restate the absence of an accepted off-road false-alarm rate.
Both recommend equal acceptance weight for nuisance and missed interventions.
Both reject warning-system equivalence as the acceptance target for automatic braking.
Both retain internal ownership of operating domain, scenarios, acceptance criteria and correlation data.
Specifies assets retained internally and why manufacturer ownership matters.
Sequential testing's advance-fix requirement supports pre-registration before hardware arrival.
Technical-authority approval adds governance to advance definition of simulation acceptance criteria.
Required pass/fail and false-positive tests do not supply a statistical acceptance target.
Without a published accepted rate, field nuisance measurements need a site-agreed threshold.
On-road failure experience supports treating nuisance interventions as central acceptance measures.
Boundary-specific safety error bounds provide a concrete alternative to fixed test counts.
Missing prescribed site counts motivates coverage-and-uncertainty stopping criteria.
Adds concrete statistical-plan and test-infrastructure deliverables to the mid-2027 readiness target.
Expands function-level validation outcomes into distinct defensible automatic-braking simulation claims.
